title: Ops parity & mitigation lanes: self-hosted inference vs Redwood
body:
Context and intent:
This is a working brief for sales + product to use when confronting engineering-heavy buyers who are seriously evaluating a self-hosted inference stack (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM combos). Aim: give pragmatic operational parity checklist, mitigation lanes (how customers can get the benefits of self-hosting while minimizing the operator tax), and sharp comms/rebuttals for common build-vs-buy objections.

TL;DR (for quick use by AE/SE):
- Self-hosted stacks look cheap on paper but hide ops, reliability, perf drift, and feature gap costs (streaming, structured outputs, rollout controls).
- Key selling thread: we deliver production-grade parity (SLOs + observability + predictable unit economics) + migration lanes (hybrid, dedicated pods, private deploy) so teams can keep control without owning the stack.
- Practical close hooks: predictable billing, rollback and canary tooling, managed kernel/quantization updates, model catalog compatibility guarantees.

Quick comparative snapshot (operator-focused):
- vLLM/TGI (OSS combo): fast to prototype, great for single-model low-concurrency experiments, lots of community config overhead. Pain points: node tuning, batch sizing, KV cache correctness, memory fragmentation, cold-starts.
- TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA optimized): best for very low-latency at scale on specific hardware. Pain points: compatibility with frequent model updates, engineering effort to maintain quantized kernels, licensing/driver complexity.
- Custom mix (vLLM + TRT): highest ops overhead; often requires dedicated infra + SRE time.
- Redwood: unified runtime that handles batching, KV cache, quantization profiles, fallback routing; product-level features (rollouts, tracing, token cost breakdowns).

Operational parity checklist (what buyers actually need vs what OSS affords):
1) Predictable tail latency under mixed request sizes (SLOs) -> OSS: manual tuning, suffers at tail. Redwood: runtime queuing + smart routing.
2) Cost per token and cost forecasting -> OSS: ad-hoc (instance hours + GPU mixes + utilization math). Redwood: per-token telemetry and forecasting.
3) Continuous model updates without downtime -> OSS: rollout scripts + heavy testing. Redwood: built-in rollouts + canary -> auto-fallback.
4) KV/prefix caching correctness under multi-tenant load -> OSS: brittle, debugging heavy. Redwood: deterministic cache logic + observability.
5) Quantization and kernel maintenance -> OSS: engineering work and frequent rebuilds. Redwood: recommended profiles + automated kernel selection.
6) Security/compliance (KMS, VPC, audit logs) -> OSS: assemble multiple tools and audit trails. Redwood Private: integrated controls and enterprise support.
7) Observability (per-route cost, token breakdowns, prompt regressions) -> OSS: DIY dashboards; often incomplete. Redwood Console: out-of-box.

Hidden cost categories (sales talking points):
- Engineering time: tuning, driver upgrades, kernel builds, CUDA patches, memory leak hunting.
- SRE burden: incident runbooks, capacity pools, autoscaling policies, emergency fallbacks.
- Model ops: conversion/quantization pipelines, fallback compat tests, packaging work to fit optimized runtimes.
- Feature gaps: streaming deltas, structured output support, function/tool-calling - take engineering cycles to implement.
- Opportunity cost: time to market for the feature that uses the model.

Concrete cost decomposition example (leave with customer):
- OSS baseline: 3-5 engineers (0.5–1 FTE SRE + 1–2 infra eng + 1 ML infra) for year 1 to reach production; hardware ops + margin add ~20–40% runtime inefficiency vs runbook-optimized managed stack.
- Redwood alternative: 0.2–0.4 FTE integration effort + predictable monthly cost and operational SLAs.
(Notes: numbers are heuristics — attach case studies where possible.)

Common buyer personas & tailored messaging:
- ML Engineer: "I want full control of kernels/quantization." Rebuttal: "We give kernel-level knobs in Redwood Optimize and let you test quantization profiles in a safe canary with per-prompt quality monitoring. You keep control of model artifacts; we manage the runtime ops."
- Platform/Infra Lead: "We can't trust a managed provider for latency SLOs or compliance." Rebuttal: "Dedicated capacity + private deployment give pinned latency and audit integrations; we provide deterministic routing and SLA-backed uptime. We also provide a hybrid lane for sensitive workloads."
- CTO/Head of Product: "Total cost is lower if we build." Rebuttal: "Factor in feature velocity, incident cost, and the cost of maintaining parity with new model formats — the runway to break-even is often 12–18 months. We have customers who migrated after initial build and saw ops overhead exceed the cost of Redwood in month X (include anonymized case fig here)."

Mitigation lanes (playbook for negotiated deployments):
1) Pilot + dual-run: Customer runs a small critical path (canary) on Redwood and the rest on OSS. We instrument delta in cost/latency and show deterministic improvements for scaling.
2) Dedicated pods: reserved capacity in Redwood Dedicated for customers who need predictable throughput; reduces jitter concerns.
3) Private plane + lift-and-shift support: for regulated customers we offer a package that accelerates on-prem adoption while keeping control-plane features.
4) Hybrid edge: edge inference stays in-customer (for latency/regulatory reasons) while model updates, rollouts, and observability are managed by Redwood (control plane).

Technical differentiators to emphasize in RFP/POC:
- Kernel/quantization ops as a product (not a project): pre-built profiles + testing harnesses.
- Smart routing/fallback: deterministic fallback to compatible model variants during capacity pressure.
- Prefix & KV caching accuracy at scale.
- Token-level cost telemetry for forecasting and chargeback.

Objection scripts (short):
- "We can tune vLLM ourselves." -> "Yes, for a narrow set of workloads. At scale you need continuous tuning; we can show the delta from a 6-week POC with a comparable config."
- "We prefer vendor lock-in avoidance." -> "We support common model formats and can export logs/metrics; migration lanes and a transparent model catalog reduce lock-in risk."
- "We have unique HW setup (on-prem GPUs)." -> "Private deployment + professional services to integrate with your hardware and drivers — we treat that as an engineering engagement rather than a product gap."

Open questions / risks to surface in pitch:
- Quantify expected break-even for customer by size: need to run quick calc per prospect (tokens/month, concurrency distribution, model size, team FTE assumptions). TODO: make a one-click calc spreadsheet and attach.
- Edge cases: extremely custom kernels or bleeding-edge academic research models where vendor-managed kernels lag. Mitigation: professional services + dedicated kernel support.
- License risk for proprietary TRT extensions: map to legal review lane.

Actionable next steps (owner + ETA):
- Build a one-page "ops parity calculator" (Priya) -> 2025-03-05
- Create SE playbook with 3 POC templates: (a) 30-day cost/latency POC, (b) canary rollout plan, (c) private deploy quickstart (Miguel) -> 2025-02-28
- Draft anonymized case study for a customer who moved from vLLM to Redwood Dedicated (Ethan) -> 2025-03-15

Notes to self / raw fragments for slide creation:
- Slide: "What customers think they need vs what they actually pay for" (two-column table).
- Quote bank: "We spent 3 months tuning and still had 2x higher tail latency during peak." (redact customer).
- Include microbenchmarks for vLLM/TGI/TensorRT in appendix — but label as "engineering sample".

References and artifacts: see linked_artifacts above. See CONFLUENCE-2289 for the internal kernel compatibility matrix and JIRA-MLOPS-1342 for POC checklist.

Status: draft. Needs SE review and an anonymized cost case to make the POC sellable.

-- Aisha
